project_scope.selection_mode: Broad Kew Boraginaceae family-first module with classic-borage, hydrophylloid, heliotrope, and Ehretia doors
project_scope.note: Project taxonomy follows the broad Boraginaceae concept used by POWO, which includes former Hydrophyllaceae. The learner therefore avoids treating rough hairs, scorpioid cymes, gynobasic styles, or four nutlets as universal family requirements.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the flower and inflorescence: usually a fused 5-lobed corolla with 5 stamens attached to the corolla tube, often in a coiled/scorpioid cyme. Then inspect the ovary, style position and fruit because the broad family contains several very different fruit plans.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Leaves are usually alternate and without stipules. Many herbaceous members are rough or bristly, but the broad family also includes smooth herbs, shrubs and trees such as Ehretia.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are usually bisexual and 5-merous with a fused corolla; stamens usually equal the corolla lobes and alternate with them. The ovary is superior and 2-carpellate, often becoming apparently 4-lobed/4-locular in classic borages.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fruit varies across the broad family: classic borages commonly make four nutlets; heliotrope relatives may split into 2–4 mericarps; Ehretia makes a fleshy drupaceous fruit; hydrophylloid genera such as Phacelia use capsules.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not memorize 'hairy + scorpioid + four nutlets' as the whole family. First decide which Boraginaceae door the plant fits.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: fused 5-part flower → inflorescence architecture → fruit/style door → local genus groups → Solanaceae/Lamiaceae tie-breakers
visual_lesson.intro: Boraginaceae makes more sense as several related visual patterns. The classic rough, coiled, four-nutlet plant is only one of them.

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the scorpioid pattern
steps.look_for: A one-sided flowering axis curled like a scorpion tail, with younger buds toward the coiled tip.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a high-value clue in many classic borages and heliotrope relatives, but it is not universal.

steps.title: 2 · Classic-borage door: find the four-part ovary/nutlets
steps.look_for: A deeply 4-lobed superior ovary with the style arising from between the lobes, later separating into up to four one-seeded nutlets.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the strongest route into Lithospermum, Cryptantha, Myosotis, Cynoglossum, Lappula and related classic borages.

steps.title: 3 · Hydrophylloid door: Phacelia, Nemophila and Nama
steps.look_for: Often showy fused 5-part flowers, but fruit is a capsule rather than four nutlets; style is terminal rather than strongly gynobasic.
steps.why_it_matters: These genera were historically taught as Hydrophyllaceae and are now inside the project's broad Boraginaceae concept.

steps.title: 4 · Heliotrope door: Heliotropium and Euploca
steps.photo_role: coiled cyme + terminal style + mericarp fruit
steps.look_for: Small fused flowers commonly arranged along coiled/circinate axes; a terminal style and fruit splitting into two or four units.
steps.why_it_matters: This separates the heliotrope architecture from the gynobasic four-nutlet classic-borage pattern.

steps.title: 5 · Ehretia door: remember the family can be a tree
steps.look_for: Woody tree/shrub habit, small cymose flowers, terminal bifid style and a fleshy drupe-like fruit whose stone can separate into smaller units.
steps.why_it_matters: Ehretia anacua prevents the learner from reducing Boraginaceae to rough little herbs.

comparisons.title: Boraginaceae vs Solanaceae
comparisons.rule: Both often have fused 5-part flowers. Classic Boraginaceae usually points toward scorpioid cymes and four nutlets; Solanaceae more often has a many-seeded berry or capsule from a usually 2-locular ovary. Broad Boraginaceae has exceptions, so fruit and style position matter.

comparisons.title: Boraginaceae vs Lamiaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can end in four nutlets. Lamiaceae usually has opposite leaves, a strongly bilabiate corolla and a 4-angled stem; classic Boraginaceae usually has alternate leaves and often a scorpioid inflorescence.

comparisons.title: Classic Boraginaceae vs hydrophylloid Boraginaceae
comparisons.rule: Classic door: gynobasic style + four nutlets. Hydrophylloid door: terminal style + capsular fruit, even though both belong to the broad family used in this project.

visual_lesson.caveat: Boraginaceae circumscription varies among references. This learner follows the broad POWO/Kew family concept, so older field guides may place Phacelia, Nemophila and Nama in Hydrophyllaceae and heliotropes in Heliotropiaceae.
